title: Latin square as a named blocking grid
dek: Wikipedia Latin square: each treatment once per row and column. A blocking tool, not a miracle against every confounder.
story: A Latin square on Wikipedia is an n×n grid of n treatments, each appearing once per row and once per column. Agronomy used rows and columns as two blocking factors. PCR plates can use row and column the same way.
It is a DoE composition, not an analysis that ignores remaining confounders (time of day, reagent lot if those are not row/column).
stats-blocking is the verb. This card is the named grid people remember from textbooks.
deep: You get n² runs for n treatments — expensive if n is a drug library.
Greco-Latin squares add a third factor with a second alphabet; aliasing gets real.
Randomise the symbols onto actual treatments; a pretty square of A–D is not itself randomisation.
TB example: 4 drugs × 4 incubators × 4 technicians is the fantasy layout; reality is messier.

visual.caption: A 4×4 Latin square drawn as a grid of treatment letters. Rows and columns are blocks; letters are treatments. Not a mutation table.

example.title: Pretty A–D square, reagents aliased with row
example.setup: Row 1 was the bad lot, all 'A' happened to be… wait, Latin square puts each treatment in each row once, so lot-as-row is blocked.

steps.title: If the bad lot is a diagonal you did not block, you lose

example.takeaway: A Latin square blocks two named factors. Unnamed factors still bite.
